# AGENT.md: make this agent's launch page from one real run

You are a coding agent working inside the repository of a product that is itself an AI agent: something that
does work on a person's behalf (writes code, drives a browser, runs ops, does research). The team picked the
**agentic** format. The page opens on a task typed into a box; Run turns the page into the run: a run sheet
streams the plan and every tool call, the agent's own labelled cursor works a desk of small windows, long waits
pass as time-lapses, it stops and asks before something risky, and it ends on a printed receipt of what it did.
The same page, opened with `?record`, is the stage they record as their launch video for X (16:9, 1:1 and 9:16).

It only works if the run is **real**. A visitor who has used agents can smell an invented trace in two seconds:
tool names nobody ships, results that are too tidy, a clock that doesn't add up. You are transcribing one real
run, not writing fiction.

Read `tour/README.md` once for the engine (especially *More than one pointer* and the three design sizes). Then:

## 0. Where things are

```
index.html          the page: the agentic section only (the receipt is the ending; there is no install band)
agentic/section.html   the desk: task box, run sheet, workspace windows, receipt, controls. Edit index.html's copy.
agentic/section.css    layout for wide (1600×900), square (760×760) and tall (480×854), tokens at the top
agentic/script.js      the run, step by step (a function of the section, so the task comes from the markup)
agentic/section.js     the live clock: speed, waiting for Run and Approve, the run clock, the receipt numbers
tour/                  the engine; don't edit
```

## 1. Harvest the run (before writing anything)

Ask the team for, or find in the repo, these four things. Each one replaces a placeholder.

1. **Their agent's real tool names and schemas.** The tool list the model is given: `tools=[…]` in the agent
   loop, an MCP server's `list_tools`, a `tools/*.ts` folder, function-calling JSON schemas. Use the exact names
   (`str_replace_based_edit_tool`, `browser.navigate`, `run_shell`, whatever they are) and the argument that
   matters most for each call (a path, a URL, a command, a query). The run sheet shows `name  short-argument`.
2. **A real run log or trace.** A saved transcript, an OpenTelemetry/Langfuse/LangSmith trace, the JSONL their
   CLI writes, a replay file, their own run-history view. Pick one run that is short (8–15 tool calls), finishes,
   has one honest stumble (a failing test, a 404, a selector that moved) and one point where it asks a person.
   Take from it: the task sentence verbatim, the plan if it makes one, each call's name, argument, result summary
   and duration, the total wall-clock time, and where the long waits were. Strip secrets, customer data and
   private names; use a demo repo or account if the real one is private.
3. **The real artefacts it produced.** The pull request, the report, the deployed page, the ticket, the CSV.
   These are the receipt's links (`pr_href`, `preview_href`, `log_href` slots) and what the windows show.
   Link to a public copy, or remove a link rather than pointing it at nothing.
4. **Their real UI for the run view, if they have one.** If the product has its own run sheet (a sidebar of
   steps, a session view, an activity feed), harvest it instead of the generic one: capture it with
   `tour/snapshot.py` into a fragment, or copy its rendered markup and built CSS, and keep the hooks
   (`data-tour="r-…"`, `@now`, `@status`, `@clock`, `@count`). The same goes for the windows: if the agent works
   in their own editor, browser panel or terminal, use theirs.

Never invent a tool, a result, a number or a quote. If the trace doesn't have it, leave it out.

## 2. Put the run in

**The task** is `{{task}}` (index.html, in three places: the run sheet header, the receipt and the Run button's
label). One sentence a person would really type. `script.js` types it from the markup.

**The plan** (`.ag-plan li`): the agent's own plan from the trace, 3–6 items. No plan in the product? Delete the
section and the `stream('.ag-plan li')` and `plan()` steps.

**The run sheet rows** (`.ag-row`, `data-tour="r-<id>"`): one per tool call, in order. Each row: number, an icon,
`.ag-tool` (the real name), `.ag-arg` (the short argument), `.ag-ms` (its real duration), `.ag-sum` (the result in
a few words) and, for the 2–4 calls that matter, `.ag-res` (the result itself, a few lines; it opens, then folds).
A failing result gets `.is-bad`, a passing one `.is-good`. The approval row is `.ag-ask`: its question must be the
one the product really asks, with the real buttons.

**The windows** (`.ag-win`): one per surface the agent touches. The placeholder has an editor (with a diff), a
terminal, a browser and docs; a research agent might have a browser, a notes doc and a spreadsheet, an ops agent a
terminal, a dashboard and a runbook. Keep 2–4. Each is a `data-chrome` window (`app`, `browser`, `terminal`), so
the engine draws its frame. Fill it with what the agent really saw and made: the real diff lines (`.ln.add`,
`.ln.del`, streamed in with `.ins`), the real terminal output, the real page. Rename `WINS` in `script.js` and the
tabs (`.ag-tabs`) to match.

**The script** (`script.js`): for each call, `...begin(id, 'what it is doing')`, the agent's pointer steps
(`{ by: 'agent', tag: '<tool name>' }`) on the window it acts in, the window's change (`stream`, `set`, `tween`),
then `...done(id)` (or `done(id, 1.6)` to open the result for 1.6 s). `...focus('editor')` shows that window (wide:
an accent ring; square and tall: it becomes the live window). One `zoom()` per window visit at most.

**Time.** The run clock in the sheet is real time from the trace, computed by `section.js`: film seconds count as
seconds, and each `...lapse(rows)` span counts as the matching entry in `lapses: [ … ]` (seconds). So every long
wait (a test suite, a build, a crawl, a deploy) becomes a `lapse()`, marked on screen as a time-lapse, and the
clock lands on the trace's real total. Make the row durations agree with it. The receipt's time comes from the
same clock; its "By hand" line (`{{by_hand}}`) must be an estimate the team will stand behind, or delete it.

**The receipt** (`.ag-receipt`): what it did in one line (the task), tool calls (counted for you), approvals,
the checks it ran, files changed with the real counts, links to the real artefacts, the time, one CTA
(`{{cta}}` → `{{cta_href}}`) and the domain. Keep it short: it's the frame people screenshot.

**Names.** `{{name}}` / `{{name_em}}`, `{{agent}}` (the label on the agent's cursor: its product name, or
"Agent"), `{{repo}}`, `{{eyebrow}}`, `{{lede}}`. Keep their own colour for `--ag` in `section.css` if the
product has one; the person stays ink. Delete every `<span class="sf-note">` and set the page `<title>`.

## 3. Check it

- `?record&ratio=16:9&t=30` freezes any moment; `?record&ratio=1:1` and `?record&ratio=9:16` are the other two
  layouts. Look at: the task typing, the first plan, every `done()` with an open result, each time-lapse, the
  failure, the approval (both cursors in frame), the receipt.
- The live page: the task types itself and waits for Run (or Enter); the run plays at 1×, 2× or 4×; at the
  approval it waits for the visitor's Approve (and after 7 s the "You" cursor approves for them); ←/→ step through
  the tool calls; the receipt's links work. Check a phone width, and reduced motion (the task, then Run shows the
  finished run).
- Nothing on the page is a tool, number or result that isn't in the trace.

## 4. Record and post

Open `index.html?record&ratio=9:16` (it reads like a phone screen-recording of the agent working), `1:1` for the
feed, `16:9` for desktop and quote posts, in a browser window big enough for a crisp stage, and record it with
Monet Shot: crop to the stage, park the real pointer off it. It holds on the empty task box for 1.2 s, plays the
whole run once with both cursors drawn, and stops on the receipt. Post it with the task sentence as the first line.

# tour.js: the demo-film engine One engine for every StyleFeatures demo film. A template supplies a window with a product inside it and a script; the engine plays it with a fake cursor, a camera, chapter cards and captions, and drives it from a scroll, a clock, a screen recorder or a frozen `?t=`. Files: | file | what it is | edit it? | |---|---|---| | `tour.js` | the engine: step builders, `Tour`, `include()` | no, it's shared by every format | | `tour.css` | the engine's look: chromes, cursor, card, caption, keys, controls, record stage | no; restyle through its tokens | | `script.js` | this film's script | yes | | `section.html` / `section.css` | this film's band, closing frame and product | yes | | `snapshot.py` | harvests a live screen into a static fragment | no | | `export.py` | copies the whole format out as a standalone folder | no | | `AGENT.md` | the brief for the coding agent that fills it in | read it | Everything on screen is a pure function of one number, `t`, in seconds. Each frame the engine works out the product's state at `t` (classes, attributes, text, CSS variables, scroll positions), the camera, the cursor and the overlays, then writes only what changed. Nothing depends on what happened in earlier frames, so any moment renders on its own, the same way every time. ## Markup ```html
… your product, built at 1200 × 750 design pixels …
…
…
``` The engine adds the chrome, the cursor, ripples, the chapter card, the caption line, key caps, and the driver's controls. The opening band (`data-tour-band`) slides away in the first `intro` seconds; the closing frame (`data-tour-end`) gets `--in` 0→1 at the end and its own CSS decides what that looks like. The root also carries `--tour-band` (1 → 0 over the intro), `--tour-out` (0 → 1 over the outro) and `--tour-p` (0 → 1 over the whole film) for a format's own CSS. `data-tour-band="css"` stops the engine sliding the band away; the format fades or moves it from `--tour-band` instead. **A frame the format draws: `data-tour-frame`.** Put an element with `data-tour-frame` in the stage and lay it out in CSS (a phone's glass, a mat around a screenshot, a different box per ratio). The engine fits the window to it exactly, clips the camera to it (with its `border-radius`), and every zoom stays inside it: the window always covers the frame, so a push-in never shows what's around it. The outro then leaves the window where it is (use `--tour-out` to do something else). Give the frame the window's aspect ratio. `demo/phone` (the glass, beside the text or under it) and `demo/launch-note` (a mat on the page, a different box per recording ratio) use it. ### Window chromes: `data-chrome` | value | looks like | typical `data-size` | |---|---|---| | `browser` | traffic lights, back/forward, an address pill (`data-url`), share/new icons | `1200x750` | | `app` | a macOS title bar with traffic lights and a centred `data-title` | `1200x760` | | `phone` | a dark bezel, a status bar with the time and a notch | `390x844` | | `none` | just rounded corners | anything | | `terminal` | a warm charcoal window, traffic lights, a centred `data-title`; tokens `--tour-term-bg/-bar/-ink/-dim` | `780x548` | **Windows inside the window.** Any element inside the window with a `data-chrome` gets that chrome too, and a frame (`display:flex`, rounded, clipped). With `data-chrome="none"` on the outer window (made transparent in your CSS) it becomes a desk holding, say, a terminal and a browser; the camera pans between them with `zoom()` (`demo/terminal` does this). **A second design size for tall stages.** `data-size-tall="440x820"` on the window (or `sizeTall: [440, 820]` in the script) is used whenever the stage is taller than wide (W/H < .8: phones, 9:16 recordings). The root gets `.is-tall` before anything is measured, so your CSS can re-lay the product for it (stack two panes, say) and the script's targets follow. `demo/split` stacks its panes this way. **A third for squarish stages.** `data-size-square="760x760"` (or `sizeSquare: [760, 760]`) is used when .8 ≤ W/H < 1.15 (1:1 recordings, square-ish windows), and the root gets `.is-square` the same way. Without it those stages use the wide size, as before. `demo/agentic` has all three: a tiled desk (wide), and one live window beside (square) or above (tall) its run sheet. **A height that follows the frame: `auto`.** `data-size="580xauto"` (or `size: [580, 'auto']`, and the same for `sizeTall`) fixes the window's width and takes its height from the `data-tour-frame` at every layout, so the window always has the frame's shape: a full-height column on a wide page, the whole screen on a phone, any recording ratio. For products that read top to bottom (a chat, a feed, a transcript). `demo/chat` and `demo/mcp` use it. Build the product at the design size in plain CSS pixels. The engine scales the whole window, so text stays real text and stays sharp at any zoom. ### Hooks `'@name'` anywhere in a selector means `[data-tour="name"]`. Put `data-tour="…"` on the things the script points at. Pointer targets also choose the cursor: links, buttons, `role=button|tab|switch` get the hand, inputs and `data-tour-cursor="text"` get the I-beam, the rest the arrow (`data-tour-cursor="arrow|pointer|text"` overrides it). While the cursor rests on a target, that target has `.is-hover`; while it's pressed, `.is-press`. Style both so clicks read. ## The script ```js import { click, type, show, hide, set, tween, zoom, unzoom, chapter, caption, pause } from './tour.js'; export default { size: [1200, 750], // window design size (or data-size on the window) enter: [.84, .97], // where the cursor comes in from, as fractions of the window intro: 1.3, // seconds for the opening band to clear (0: no band) outro: 4.5, // seconds held on the closing frame settle: .6, // pause between the last step and the outro still: 17.4, // the moment reduced motion shows fit: [.92, .88, .5], // optional: see below steps: [ … ], }; ``` `fit: [w, h, y]` is for a stage that holds nothing but the window (a panel beside text, with no card or band over it): the window may take `w` of the stage's width and `h` of its height, centred at `y` (default .5), and push-ins aim at the middle of the frame. Without it the page layout leaves room for the card and band (`[.74, .7, .47]`). It never changes `?record`. `demo/chapters` uses it. Steps run in order on one clock. **Pointer steps** take time and the next step waits for them. **Side steps** start at the current moment and the next step starts with them, so `click('@create'), hide('@modal'), show('@toast')` hides the modal and shows the toast as the click lands. Every step takes: `at: 12.5` pin it to an absolute time · `wait: .4` start this much later · `parallel: true` (pointer steps) don't hold up the next step · `block: true` (side steps) do hold it up. ### Pointer steps | step | what happens | options (defaults) | |---|---|---| | `move(sel)` | glides there on a gentle arc, smootherstep | `dur` .9, `aim` [x, y] fractions of the target, `cursor` | | `click(sel)` | moves, presses (cursor shrinks, target gets `.is-press`), ripple | as `move` | | `dblclick(sel)` | moves, two presses, two ripples | as `move` | | `hover(sel)` | moves and rests (`.is-hover` on the target) | `dur` .9, `hold` .6 | | `type(sel, text)` | characters appear in `sel` at a human, uneven pace; `.is-caret` while typing, then blinking | `cps` 13, `rhythm` (below), `lead` (s of steady caret before the first key), `caret` (s it blinks after the last key, 1.6), `blink` (absolute time it goes) | | `stream(sel)` | each match appears in turn, like output arriving: gets `.is-in`, and `--in` 0→1 over `dur`. A match's `data-tour-wait="1.2"` adds that pause before it (a slow step) | `every` .06 s, `jitter` .5 (±50 % of `every`; 0 for an exact beat), `dur` .08 | | `drag(handle, o)` | moves to the handle, presses, then drives a value while the cursor stays on the handle | `approach` .8, `dur` 1.2, `prop` + `from` + `to` (+ `el` to put the property on another element), `text: [sel, v => label]`, or `onto: sel` to carry the handle itself there | | `scroll(sel, to)` | scrolls an element; `to` is px, `'50%'`, `'end'` or a selector inside it | `dur` 1.4, `offset` 16 | | `key(keys)` | key caps on screen, e.g. `key(['⌘', 'K'])` | `dur` .9, `hold` 1.4 | | `pause(s)` | a beat | | | `tap(sel)` | the same step as `click`; reads better in a touch film | as `click` | | `longpress(sel)` | moves, presses and holds; it fires (`.is-press` stays on, a ripple) after `hold`, and the finger stays down `lift` longer while the next steps start (open a context menu there) | `dur` .9, `hold` .7, `lift` .35 | | `swipe(sel, o)` | a finger flick that starts on `sel`: lands, travels `by` [dx, dy] window px speeding up, lifts while still moving. What it moves follows it 1:1, then coasts to rest over `coast` s with the speed it was let go at. `scroll: to` scrolls `sel` (or `in: sel`) to `to` (px, `'50%'`, `'end'`, a selector; `offset`); `prop` + `from` + `to` (+ `el`) drives a CSS variable instead (a carousel, a sheet dragged down), `follow` (.45) of it under the finger | `approach` .7, `by` [0, -220], `dur` .36, `coast` .8 (0: a slow drag that ends at rest), `settle` (when the next step starts, `coast` × .5) | `type`'s `rhythm`: unset is the even, slightly uneven pace it always had. `'human'` types like a person at a keyboard: a beat between words, a reach for symbols (`- / . : =`), a pause after punctuation, doubled letters run together, the odd hesitation. `'stream'` lands the text in chunks of 1–5 characters, the way a model's reply arrives. `stream()` is for whole lines or blocks; hide them in CSS until `.is-in` (`.line{display:none}.line.is-in{display:block}`) so they take space only once they've arrived. The cursor's path between targets is a smootherstep glide with a slight bow (direction-dependent, never a straight line) and a slightly early peak speed, like a hand. It never teleports: each move starts where the last one ended. **A finger instead of a cursor.** `pointer: 'touch'` in the script (or `data-pointer="touch"` on the root, `?pointer=touch`) swaps the arrow for a fingertip: a soft translucent dot, 44 window px, that is part of the screen, so it zooms with it. It is unseen between touches (a hand travelling isn't on the glass); a shadow gathers for a fifth of a second before contact, the dot flattens and darkens while pressed (`.is-down` on `.tour-cur`), and lifts away. `drag` and `swipe` carry it across the glass. Give each touch a beat: the `dur` before it is the hand travelling. Restyle the dot with `--tour-touch` / `--tour-touch-down`. `demo/phone` is the worked example. **More than one pointer.** Any pointer step with `by: 'agent'` moves a second cursor on its own track (any name works; steps without `by` move the usual one, `'main'`). Describe each in the script: ```js pointers: { main: { label: 'You', idle: 1.4 }, // a tag on the person's cursor; it fades after 1.4 s still agent: { label: 'Agent', look: 'agent', bow: .2, enter: [.33, .2] }, }, steps: [ click('@search', { by: 'agent', tag: 'search_code' }), …, click('@approve', { from: [.99, 1.03] }) ] ``` A second pointer is an arrow in `--tour-agent` (look `'agent'`) with a label tag beside it; `tag` on a step adds a word to that label from then on (the tool it's using, "waiting for you"). `bow` scales the curve of its path (0 is a straight, machine-like line), `enter` is where it first appears, `shapes: true` lets it take the hand and I-beam too. `idle: s` fades a pointer out once it has been still that long and back in when it next moves; `from: [x, y]` (fractions of the window) on a step starts that move there instead, so a hand can come back in from off the edge. Each pointer's clicks ripple in its own colour (`.tour-ring[data-who]`), and `.tour-cur[data-who="…"]` lets a page hide one (`demo/agentic` hides the person's cursor on the live page, where the visitor is the person). Zoom levels move on a log scale, so in and out feel even. Numbers are multiplied by 1.15 on portrait stages, where the window is small (not inside a `data-tour-frame`, which the window always fills). `?camera=off` turns all push-ins off. On stacked stages (1:1, 9:16, phones) the cursor fades out rather than being drawn outside the window's frame. ### Measuring Targets are measured in the window's own pixels, against the product as it is at the moment each step happens (so a button inside a modal that opens two steps earlier is measured with the modal open), and measured again whenever the layout can change: fonts loading, the stage resizing, your CSS. # AGENT.md: make this agent's launch page from one real run

You are a coding agent working inside the repository of a product that is itself an AI agent: something that
does work on a person's behalf (writes code, drives a browser, runs ops, does research). The team picked the
**agentic** format. The page opens on a task typed into a box; Run turns the page into the run: a run sheet
streams the plan and every tool call, the agent's own labelled cursor works a desk of small windows, long waits
pass as time-lapses, it stops and asks before something risky, and it ends on a printed receipt of what it did.
The same page, opened with `?record`, is the stage they record as their launch video for X (16:9, 1:1 and 9:16).

It only works if the run is **real**. A visitor who has used agents can smell an invented trace in two seconds:
tool names nobody ships, results that are too tidy, a clock that doesn't add up. You are transcribing one real
run, not writing fiction.

Read `tour/README.md` once for the engine (especially *More than one pointer* and the three design sizes). Then:

## 0. Where things are

```
index.html          the page: the agentic section only (the receipt is the ending; there is no install band)
agentic/section.html   the desk: task box, run sheet, workspace windows, receipt, controls. Edit index.html's copy.
agentic/section.css    layout for wide (1600×900), square (760×760) and tall (480×854), tokens at the top
agentic/script.js      the run, step by step (a function of the section, so the task comes from the markup)
agentic/section.js     the live clock: speed, waiting for Run and Approve, the run clock, the receipt numbers
tour/                  the engine; don't edit
```

## 1. Harvest the run (before writing anything)

Ask the team for, or find in the repo, these four things. Each one replaces a placeholder.

1. **Their agent's real tool names and schemas.** The tool list the model is given: `tools=[…]` in the agent
   loop, an MCP server's `list_tools`, a `tools/*.ts` folder, function-calling JSON schemas. Use the exact names
   (`str_replace_based_edit_tool`, `browser.navigate`, `run_shell`, whatever they are) and the argument that
   matters most for each call (a path, a URL, a command, a query). The run sheet shows `name  short-argument`.
2. **A real run log or trace.** A saved transcript, an OpenTelemetry/Langfuse/LangSmith trace, the JSONL their
   CLI writes, a replay file, their own run-history view. Pick one run that is short (8–15 tool calls), finishes,
   has one honest stumble (a failing test, a 404, a selector that moved) and one point where it asks a person.
   Take from it: the task sentence verbatim, the plan if it makes one, each call's name, argument, result summary
   and duration, the total wall-clock time, and where the long waits were. Strip secrets, customer data and
   private names; use a demo repo or account if the real one is private.
3. **The real artefacts it produced.** The pull request, the report, the deployed page, the ticket, the CSV.
   These are the receipt's links (`pr_href`, `preview_href`, `log_href` slots) and what the windows show.
   Link to a public copy, or remove a link rather than pointing it at nothing.
4. **Their real UI for the run view, if they have one.** If the product has its own run sheet (a sidebar of
   steps, a session view, an activity feed), harvest it instead of the generic one: capture it with
   `tour/snapshot.py` into a fragment, or copy its rendered markup and built CSS, and keep the hooks
   (`data-tour="r-…"`, `@now`, `@status`, `@clock`, `@count`). The same goes for the windows: if the agent works
   in their own editor, browser panel or terminal, use theirs.

Never invent a tool, a result, a number or a quote. If the trace doesn't have it, leave it out.

## 2. Put the run in

**The task** is `{{task}}` (index.html, in three places: the run sheet header, the receipt and the Run button's
label). One sentence a person would really type. `script.js` types it from the markup.

**The plan** (`.ag-plan li`): the agent's own plan from the trace, 3–6 items. No plan in the product? Delete the
section and the `stream('.ag-plan li')` and `plan()` steps.

**The run sheet rows** (`.ag-row`, `data-tour="r-<id>"`): one per tool call, in order. Each row: number, an icon,
`.ag-tool` (the real name), `.ag-arg` (the short argument), `.ag-ms` (its real duration), `.ag-sum` (the result in
a few words) and, for the 2–4 calls that matter, `.ag-res` (the result itself, a few lines; it opens, then folds).
A failing result gets `.is-bad`, a passing one `.is-good`. The approval row is `.ag-ask`: its question must be the
one the product really asks, with the real buttons.

**The windows** (`.ag-win`): one per surface the agent touches. The placeholder has an editor (with a diff), a
terminal, a browser and docs; a research agent might have a browser, a notes doc and a spreadsheet, an ops agent a
terminal, a dashboard and a runbook. Keep 2–4. Each is a `data-chrome` window (`app`, `browser`, `terminal`), so
the engine draws its frame. Fill it with what the agent really saw and made: the real diff lines (`.ln.add`,
`.ln.del`, streamed in with `.ins`), the real terminal output, the real page. Rename `WINS` in `script.js` and the
tabs (`.ag-tabs`) to match.

**The script** (`script.js`): for each call, `...begin(id, 'what it is doing')`, the agent's pointer steps
(`{ by: 'agent', tag: '<tool name>' }`) on the window it acts in, the window's change (`stream`, `set`, `tween`),
then `...done(id)` (or `done(id, 1.6)` to open the result for 1.6 s). `...focus('editor')` shows that window (wide:
an accent ring; square and tall: it becomes the live window). One `zoom()` per window visit at most.

**Time.** The run clock in the sheet is real time from the trace, computed by `section.js`: film seconds count as
seconds, and each `...lapse(rows)` span counts as the matching entry in `lapses: [ … ]` (seconds). So every long
wait (a test suite, a build, a crawl, a deploy) becomes a `lapse()`, marked on screen as a time-lapse, and the
clock lands on the trace's real total. Make the row durations agree with it. The receipt's time comes from the
same clock; its "By hand" line (`{{by_hand}}`) must be an estimate the team will stand behind, or delete it.

**The receipt** (`.ag-receipt`): what it did in one line (the task), tool calls (counted for you), approvals,
the checks it ran, files changed with the real counts, links to the real artefacts, the time, one CTA
(`{{cta}}` → `{{cta_href}}`) and the domain. Keep it short: it's the frame people screenshot.

**Names.** `{{name}}` / `{{name_em}}`, `{{agent}}` (the label on the agent's cursor: its product name, or
"Agent"), `{{repo}}`, `{{eyebrow}}`, `{{lede}}`. Keep their own colour for `--ag` in `section.css` if the
product has one; the person stays ink. Delete every `<span class="sf-note">` and set the page `<title>`.

## 3. Check it

- `?record&ratio=16:9&t=30` freezes any moment; `?record&ratio=1:1` and `?record&ratio=9:16` are the other two
  layouts. Look at: the task typing, the first plan, every `done()` with an open result, each time-lapse, the
  failure, the approval (both cursors in frame), the receipt.
- The live page: the task types itself and waits for Run (or Enter); the run plays at 1×, 2× or 4×; at the
  approval it waits for the visitor's Approve (and after 7 s the "You" cursor approves for them); ←/→ step through
  the tool calls; the receipt's links work. Check a phone width, and reduced motion (the task, then Run shows the
  finished run).
- Nothing on the page is a tool, number or result that isn't in the trace.

## 4. Record and post

Open `index.html?record&ratio=9:16` (it reads like a phone screen-recording of the agent working), `1:1` for the
feed, `16:9` for desktop and quote posts, in a browser window big enough for a crisp stage, and record it with
Monet Shot: crop to the stage, park the real pointer off it. It holds on the empty task box for 1.2 s, plays the
whole run once with both cursors drawn, and stops on the receipt. Post it with the task sentence as the first line.

# tour.js: the demo-film engine One engine for every StyleFeatures demo film. A template supplies a window with a product inside it and a script; the engine plays it with a fake cursor, a camera, chapter cards and captions, and drives it from a scroll, a clock, a screen recorder or a frozen `?t=`. Files: | file | what it is | edit it? | |---|---|---| | `tour.js` | the engine: step builders, `Tour`, `include()` | no, it's shared by every format | | `tour.css` | the engine's look: chromes, cursor, card, caption, keys, controls, record stage | no; restyle through its tokens | | `script.js` | this film's script | yes | | `section.html` / `section.css` | this film's band, closing frame and product | yes | | `snapshot.py` | harvests a live screen into a static fragment | no | | `export.py` | copies the whole format out as a standalone folder | no | | `AGENT.md` | the brief for the coding agent that fills it in | read it | Everything on screen is a pure function of one number, `t`, in seconds. Each frame the engine works out the product's state at `t` (classes, attributes, text, CSS variables, scroll positions), the camera, the cursor and the overlays, then writes only what changed. Nothing depends on what happened in earlier frames, so any moment renders on its own, the same way every time. ## Markup ```html
… your product, built at 1200 × 750 design pixels …
…
…
``` The engine adds the chrome, the cursor, ripples, the chapter card, the caption line, key caps, and the driver's controls. The opening band (`data-tour-band`) slides away in the first `intro` seconds; the closing frame (`data-tour-end`) gets `--in` 0→1 at the end and its own CSS decides what that looks like. The root also carries `--tour-band` (1 → 0 over the intro), `--tour-out` (0 → 1 over the outro) and `--tour-p` (0 → 1 over the whole film) for a format's own CSS. `data-tour-band="css"` stops the engine sliding the band away; the format fades or moves it from `--tour-band` instead. **A frame the format draws: `data-tour-frame`.** Put an element with `data-tour-frame` in the stage and lay it out in CSS (a phone's glass, a mat around a screenshot, a different box per ratio). The engine fits the window to it exactly, clips the camera to it (with its `border-radius`), and every zoom stays inside it: the window always covers the frame, so a push-in never shows what's around it. The outro then leaves the window where it is (use `--tour-out` to do something else). Give the frame the window's aspect ratio. `demo/phone` (the glass, beside the text or under it) and `demo/launch-note` (a mat on the page, a different box per recording ratio) use it. ### Window chromes: `data-chrome` | value | looks like | typical `data-size` | |---|---|---| | `browser` | traffic lights, back/forward, an address pill (`data-url`), share/new icons | `1200x750` | | `app` | a macOS title bar with traffic lights and a centred `data-title` | `1200x760` | | `phone` | a dark bezel, a status bar with the time and a notch | `390x844` | | `none` | just rounded corners | anything | | `terminal` | a warm charcoal window, traffic lights, a centred `data-title`; tokens `--tour-term-bg/-bar/-ink/-dim` | `780x548` | **Windows inside the window.** Any element inside the window with a `data-chrome` gets that chrome too, and a frame (`display:flex`, rounded, clipped). With `data-chrome="none"` on the outer window (made transparent in your CSS) it becomes a desk holding, say, a terminal and a browser; the camera pans between them with `zoom()` (`demo/terminal` does this). **A second design size for tall stages.** `data-size-tall="440x820"` on the window (or `sizeTall: [440, 820]` in the script) is used whenever the stage is taller than wide (W/H < .8: phones, 9:16 recordings). The root gets `.is-tall` before anything is measured, so your CSS can re-lay the product for it (stack two panes, say) and the script's targets follow. `demo/split` stacks its panes this way. **A third for squarish stages.** `data-size-square="760x760"` (or `sizeSquare: [760, 760]`) is used when .8 ≤ W/H < 1.15 (1:1 recordings, square-ish windows), and the root gets `.is-square` the same way. Without it those stages use the wide size, as before. `demo/agentic` has all three: a tiled desk (wide), and one live window beside (square) or above (tall) its run sheet. **A height that follows the frame: `auto`.** `data-size="580xauto"` (or `size: [580, 'auto']`, and the same for `sizeTall`) fixes the window's width and takes its height from the `data-tour-frame` at every layout, so the window always has the frame's shape: a full-height column on a wide page, the whole screen on a phone, any recording ratio. For products that read top to bottom (a chat, a feed, a transcript). `demo/chat` and `demo/mcp` use it. Build the product at the design size in plain CSS pixels. The engine scales the whole window, so text stays real text and stays sharp at any zoom. ### Hooks `'@name'` anywhere in a selector means `[data-tour="name"]`. Put `data-tour="…"` on the things the script points at. Pointer targets also choose the cursor: links, buttons, `role=button|tab|switch` get the hand, inputs and `data-tour-cursor="text"` get the I-beam, the rest the arrow (`data-tour-cursor="arrow|pointer|text"` overrides it). While the cursor rests on a target, that target has `.is-hover`; while it's pressed, `.is-press`. Style both so clicks read. ## The script ```js import { click, type, show, hide, set, tween, zoom, unzoom, chapter, caption, pause } from './tour.js'; export default { size: [1200, 750], // window design size (or data-size on the window) enter: [.84, .97], // where the cursor comes in from, as fractions of the window intro: 1.3, // seconds for the opening band to clear (0: no band) outro: 4.5, // seconds held on the closing frame settle: .6, // pause between the last step and the outro still: 17.4, // the moment reduced motion shows fit: [.92, .88, .5], // optional: see below steps: [ … ], }; ``` `fit: [w, h, y]` is for a stage that holds nothing but the window (a panel beside text, with no card or band over it): the window may take `w` of the stage's width and `h` of its height, centred at `y` (default .5), and push-ins aim at the middle of the frame. Without it the page layout leaves room for the card and band (`[.74, .7, .47]`). It never changes `?record`. `demo/chapters` uses it. Steps run in order on one clock. **Pointer steps** take time and the next step waits for them. **Side steps** start at the current moment and the next step starts with them, so `click('@create'), hide('@modal'), show('@toast')` hides the modal and shows the toast as the click lands. Every step takes: `at: 12.5` pin it to an absolute time · `wait: .4` start this much later · `parallel: true` (pointer steps) don't hold up the next step · `block: true` (side steps) do hold it up. ### Pointer steps | step | what happens | options (defaults) | |---|---|---| | `move(sel)` | glides there on a gentle arc, smootherstep | `dur` .9, `aim` [x, y] fractions of the target, `cursor` | | `click(sel)` | moves, presses (cursor shrinks, target gets `.is-press`), ripple | as `move` | | `dblclick(sel)` | moves, two presses, two ripples | as `move` | | `hover(sel)` | moves and rests (`.is-hover` on the target) | `dur` .9, `hold` .6 | | `type(sel, text)` | characters appear in `sel` at a human, uneven pace; `.is-caret` while typing, then blinking | `cps` 13, `rhythm` (below), `lead` (s of steady caret before the first key), `caret` (s it blinks after the last key, 1.6), `blink` (absolute time it goes) | | `stream(sel)` | each match appears in turn, like output arriving: gets `.is-in`, and `--in` 0→1 over `dur`. A match's `data-tour-wait="1.2"` adds that pause before it (a slow step) | `every` .06 s, `jitter` .5 (±50 % of `every`; 0 for an exact beat), `dur` .08 | | `drag(handle, o)` | moves to the handle, presses, then drives a value while the cursor stays on the handle | `approach` .8, `dur` 1.2, `prop` + `from` + `to` (+ `el` to put the property on another element), `text: [sel, v => label]`, or `onto: sel` to carry the handle itself there | | `scroll(sel, to)` | scrolls an element; `to` is px, `'50%'`, `'end'` or a selector inside it | `dur` 1.4, `offset` 16 | | `key(keys)` | key caps on screen, e.g. `key(['⌘', 'K'])` | `dur` .9, `hold` 1.4 | | `pause(s)` | a beat | | | `tap(sel)` | the same step as `click`; reads better in a touch film | as `click` | | `longpress(sel)` | moves, presses and holds; it fires (`.is-press` stays on, a ripple) after `hold`, and the finger stays down `lift` longer while the next steps start (open a context menu there) | `dur` .9, `hold` .7, `lift` .35 | | `swipe(sel, o)` | a finger flick that starts on `sel`: lands, travels `by` [dx, dy] window px speeding up, lifts while still moving. What it moves follows it 1:1, then coasts to rest over `coast` s with the speed it was let go at. `scroll: to` scrolls `sel` (or `in: sel`) to `to` (px, `'50%'`, `'end'`, a selector; `offset`); `prop` + `from` + `to` (+ `el`) drives a CSS variable instead (a carousel, a sheet dragged down), `follow` (.45) of it under the finger | `approach` .7, `by` [0, -220], `dur` .36, `coast` .8 (0: a slow drag that ends at rest), `settle` (when the next step starts, `coast` × .5) | `type`'s `rhythm`: unset is the even, slightly uneven pace it always had. `'human'` types like a person at a keyboard: a beat between words, a reach for symbols (`- / . : =`), a pause after punctuation, doubled letters run together, the odd hesitation. `'stream'` lands the text in chunks of 1–5 characters, the way a model's reply arrives. `stream()` is for whole lines or blocks; hide them in CSS until `.is-in` (`.line{display:none}.line.is-in{display:block}`) so they take space only once they've arrived. The cursor's path between targets is a smootherstep glide with a slight bow (direction-dependent, never a straight line) and a slightly early peak speed, like a hand. It never teleports: each move starts where the last one ended. **A finger instead of a cursor.** `pointer: 'touch'` in the script (or `data-pointer="touch"` on the root, `?pointer=touch`) swaps the arrow for a fingertip: a soft translucent dot, 44 window px, that is part of the screen, so it zooms with it. It is unseen between touches (a hand travelling isn't on the glass); a shadow gathers for a fifth of a second before contact, the dot flattens and darkens while pressed (`.is-down` on `.tour-cur`), and lifts away. `drag` and `swipe` carry it across the glass. Give each touch a beat: the `dur` before it is the hand travelling. Restyle the dot with `--tour-touch` / `--tour-touch-down`. `demo/phone` is the worked example. **More than one pointer.** Any pointer step with `by: 'agent'` moves a second cursor on its own track (any name works; steps without `by` move the usual one, `'main'`). Describe each in the script: ```js pointers: { main: { label: 'You', idle: 1.4 }, // a tag on the person's cursor; it fades after 1.4 s still agent: { label: 'Agent', look: 'agent', bow: .2, enter: [.33, .2] }, }, steps: [ click('@search', { by: 'agent', tag: 'search_code' }), …, click('@approve', { from: [.99, 1.03] }) ] ``` A second pointer is an arrow in `--tour-agent` (look `'agent'`) with a label tag beside it; `tag` on a step adds a word to that label from then on (the tool it's using, "waiting for you"). `bow` scales the curve of its path (0 is a straight, machine-like line), `enter` is where it first appears, `shapes: true` lets it take the hand and I-beam too. `idle: s` fades a pointer out once it has been still that long and back in when it next moves; `from: [x, y]` (fractions of the window) on a step starts that move there instead, so a hand can come back in from off the edge. The default is smootherstep. The curves are exported as `eases`. `data-tour-follow` on a scrolling element (a terminal, a chat thread, a log) keeps its newest content in view every frame, so lines that `stream()` in push the old ones up. `data-tour-grow` on an element that should take height as it arrives (a message in a thread, a folded panel): the engine measures its natural height into `--h` (design px, innermost first, before targets are measured, and again on every relayout), so your CSS can open it with `--in` and let go once it's in: `max-height: max(calc(var(--in) * var(--h)), calc((var(--in) - .999) * 1e7px))`. Rows arrive smoothly and may change size afterwards. `../_chat/chat.css` is the worked example. Elements that `show()` controls should start hidden in CSS (`--in: 0`). Anything the script changes is reset when you seek backwards, because every value is recomputed from `t`. ### The camera `zoom` pushes in on a point and keeps the window filling the frame: it borrows Monet Shot's fit clamp, so a push-in never pans past the window's edge (the window is either wholly inside the frame or covers it). Zoom levels move on a log scale, so in and out feel even. Numbers are multiplied by 1.15 on portrait stages, where the window is small (not inside a `data-tour-frame`, which the window always fills). `?camera=off` turns all push-ins off. On stacked stages (1:1, 9:16, phones) the cursor fades out rather than being drawn outside the window's frame. ### Measuring Targets are measured in the window's own pixels, against the product as it is at the moment each step happens (so a button inside a modal that opens two steps earlier is measured with the modal open), and measured again whenever the layout can change: fonts loading, the stage resizing, your CSS. Edit the product freely; the script follows. ## Drivers | driver | how | when | |---|---|---| | `scroll` (default) | `data-driver="scroll"`. The section gets tall, the stage pins, scroll maps to `t`. The gate starts an auto-play drift at real speed. With `data-lock` (default on) wheel, touch and keys can't skip the film while it drifts; the Auto-play switch is the way out. A film at the very top of the page holds the page still until the first click, tap or key. | the opening of a launch page, Monet Shot style | | `play` | `data-driver="play"`. Record it with **Monet Shot**: pick the browser window, crop to the stage, and export. Two things to know: - Monet Shot zooms on **real** clicks. The tour's clicks are drawn, not real, so Monet Shot sees none and adds no zooms of its own. The tour's camera therefore stays **on** by default. If you would rather place zooms yourself on Monet Shot's timeline, use `&camera=off` and you won't get double zooms. - Monet Shot draws its own cursor from the real pointer. Park the real pointer off the recorded window (or set Monet Shot's cursor to hidden) so only the tour's cursor shows. From script: `window.tour` has `seek(t)`, `play()`, `pause()`, `load(script)`, `t`, `duration`, `chapters` and `ready` (a promise that resolves once fonts are in and everything is measured). The root gets a `tour:end` event whenever `play()` reaches the end (any driver). **Several tours in one recorded frame.** A format whose recording is more than one film (two windows racing in `demo/versus`, a whole slide deck in `demo/deck`) makes its own element the record stage and drives the tours itself: ```js import { Tour, recordStage } from './tour.js'; const box = q.has('record') ? recordStage(root) : null; // root becomes the ratio's box, centred on near-black, the rest hidden const a = new Tour(filmA, scriptA, { driver: 'manual', record: 'page' }); // no record stage or auto-play of its own a.render(t); // the page decides t, every frame ``` `recordStage(el)` does for `el` what `?record` does for a single film (the `tour-record` and `sf-clean` classes, `--rw`/`--rh` from `&ratio=`, kept current on resize) and returns `{ w, h, ratio }`. `{ record: 'page' }` on a Tour means: in `?record` stay on the manual driver and let the page play it (captions follow `captions` as usual). Without `?record` it changes nothing. The page then holds the first frame, plays once and honours `&t=` itself. `load(script)` swaps in another script on the same window: every value the old script touched goes back to how the page drew it, then the new script is compiled and measured. `demo/playground` uses it to turn a visitor's clicks into a live script that the engine plays on from, so their clicks get the film's eases. ## Harvested screens: `include()` and `snapshot.py` ```html
